Messages.Body:
On winning strategies and how to apply them.

Would you build a dominate deck and not use Deflection/Redirection? Or
an auspex deck and not use Telepathic Misdirection/My Enemy's Enemy?
Would you have 4+ Princes in your crypt and not use 2nd Tradition? I
wouldn't, because those cards win you games- yet at every tournament I
go to I see people going for what I have started to call 'the
enlightenment victory'.

For those of you not aware, in L5R you can win a game by getting all 5
elemental ring cards on the table at once. The rings, individually, do
very little yet together they make you win. Every time I go to Watford
or Portsmouth (or every other deck list I see posted to the group for
that matter) seems to be trying to do this in V:TES. You know the sort
of thing I'm talking about, the guy across the table from you busts
out his Tremere Convocation, Arcane library, Spirit Summoning Chamber
and Wasserschloss Anif, Austria. You start to think 'damnit- that's
one VP my prey's just got'. Low and behold the guy goes down with a
bemused look on his face saying something like:

"Aww, I was so close! Next turn I would've got out Thadius Zho!"

Ground breaking. I mean that would've made all the difference right?
The other players would take one look at the awesome powerhouse you've
assembled and think 'woah- I'm outgunned here'. No. What happened was
that the good players on the table saw what you were doing and started
to weep openly. I played a game the other night with a guy that can
build decks and play well, but found himself at 10 pool with one
minion continuously hunting with XTC Laced Blood. Did he influence out
another vampire? Nope- he sat there (whilst his predator did nothing
to him for four turns) and hunted. His reasoning? He needed that
particular vampire to use a particular card combo and now he couldn't
do that there was no point influencing another vampire out.

Now, don't get me wrong I love the way that there are no 'net decks'
in V:TES. There is no 'best deck concept'. The multiplayer aspect and
the wide variety of metagaming mean that knowing the environment
probably counts for more than in any other CCG. This is no excuse,
however, for the standard of decks that I see people playing. Newbies
with precons? Fine, not a problem. At least they are learning. Players
with 40+ games under their belts playing assamite politics? Get the
hell out of my recreational pastime.

What are you looking to change the world? Did you think that hey, just
this once having a deck with no bleed bounce or intercept will work?
I'll give you a clue shall I. No! You'll get boned. But not only will
you get boned, you'll distort the table dynamic for other people. I'm
willing to accept that people make mistakes in deck choice- as long as
they learn from it. However, there are people I play against at every
tournament that seem to be incapable of doing so. You can bet your
life that they will turn up playing the same old pile of bull that
apparently 'beat all my other decks at home' only to get aced in
record time by a deck that they will then denounce as 'sleazy'.

Newsflash: 'Effective' does not always equal 'sleazy'.

Playing dominate cards does not put you in league with the devil.
There are some tactics that you much account for when building a deck,
like it or not. And the feeling you get when you beat the weenie
dominate bleed decks id a lot better than the one you get after being
smacked by one for the fifth time in a row. And it doesn't mean to say
that your deck can't be creative. V:TES has some of the most varied
and creative competitive decks. Don't abuse the privilege.

mattgreen.

"Andy Brown" <a...@sanger.ac.uk> wrote

> People are
> also limited by their cardstock, but less so than Magic, and more
> inventive ways of using the cards (new deck ideas) should be the way
> forward.

Disagree. Magic's 4 card limit helped level the playing field
for those competitors who didn't have an unlimited supply
of cards. As did the Type I / Type II distinctions, but in
a perverse way (those who had a lot of old cards suffered,
those who could afford to constantly accumulate new cards
were advantaged, that's what you get when you let WotC
control the DCI).

Jyhad, with its no card limit, no excluded sets tournamnet
environment gives a distinct advantage to those players with
a substantial collection, as they have more deck-construction
resources available than other players (I own a lot of cards, but
I can't come close to making a 10 Disarm weenie potence
deck, or a Super Freak Drive deck).

I'm not in any way advocating card limits or set exclusion
in V:teS, but I do insist that the lack of those characteristics
in constructed tournament rules enhances the advantages of
players who own more cards.

- Jason Bell

If you think you're just as likely to win whether you can make Noal's
deck in particular, I have no reason to doubt that.

level of access to cards, you are wrong. The illustration is elementary
at the extreme, all must agree that someone with only a clan deck and
three boosters will not fare well in the midst of a constructed deck
tournament, and certainly not as well as that same player would fare
if provided with additional resources to make the deck better.

Perhaps one can delude oneself into believing that this is no longer
true as access to card resources increases, but the principle is
the same, the effect is just less pronounced. As an example,
consider the Magic player who has 4 of every card legal for
tournament play, plus lands to his heart's content. He can make
any tournament deck of which he can conceive. Compare to the
V:tES player with access to 4 of every card legal for tournament
play, plus vampires to his heart's content (mmmm, if only). That
player cannot make the best deck he can conceive. Thus my
disagreement that Magic is more dependent on cardstock than
Jyhad.

The point here is difficult, because of the fact that a number of games
- like Magic - have worked on the principle that rarity *is* a factor in
the power:cost ratio. Jyhad very consciously did not for virtually
every card.

If you work under the assumption that a rare card, in Magic, will be
better than a corresponding common card, you'll find that the rich
players again "win" - because, chances are, they've got a few more
copies of key rares knocking around than the poorer player who scraped
together those 4 copies after much searching.

More recent sets may have helped temper this to some extent, my
familiarity with recent sets of Magic isn't enough to comment.

as that Derange deck, even though it does something entirely different. If
my focus is simply to win the tournament, I shouldn't care what deck I do
it with; as long as I can successfully construct a tier 1 deck, I'll have
as good a chance as anyone. (Seating arrangements, obviously, will play a
large part in things; if I've built a Ventrue Law Firm and sit behind a

a weenie OBF Night Moves swarm deck, I'm likely to completely roll over
it.)

> clan deck and three boosters will not fare well in the midst of a

No, this is true. But one has to also set a reasonable minimum on the
amount of resources a player HAS, too. Someone with only one pre-con and
three boosters has spent less than $20 on the game, which is frankly, not a
reasonable minimum. This may not be as expensive a game as Magic, but a
tournament is not the 'have fun with my 3 friends!' level of the game,
either.

In pool, a similar analogy is "it's not the stick, it's the shooter." This
is true on the face of it; I can pick up a bent bar cue and still soundly
trounce the average player. But by the same token, if I walk into a
tournament with that bent bar cue, I'm going to be rapidly wishing I had
brought my Joss; when the players are equal, the equipment DOES start to
matter. This analogy sort of supports both sides of the argument, but
points out that you simply can't EXPECT to be tournament-competitive with
only the bare minimum of investment. (a bar cue, ironically, costs $10-$20
new.) However, I can walk into that same tournament with my $100 Viking
with the extra-tacky bright-red Grateful Dead skeleton decals on it and do
just fine, because I've gotten myself up to the REASONABLE minimum of
investment. The advantage the Joss gives me is slight, but not TOO
significant.

However, you can buy two boxes of Jyhad boosters for $60 and be in pretty
damn good shape; you'll definitely be able to make SOMETHING that's
competitive out of it, and quite a number of other "fun" decks to play in

necessary. And, for a minor additional outlay, you can put in some of the
SW/FN toys from the precons.

The point, which needs to be carefully delineated, is very unsteady when
presented solely as variety. The number of different decks and deck
strategies available also contributes to "variety".

xCL attempts to stop one trick pony style decks. (It fails because of
the Stealth and Bleed archetype, where multiples of most of the
important cards can be found.)

xCL also stifles variety by making it impossible to see an effective
Corruption deck (*slightly* more possible with Venenation and Nefertiti,
but still difficult to focus a deck around), or a Betrayer deck or many
other decks which rely around specific cards which *don't* have close
replacements available.

DISCLAIMER: SIMILAR ARGUMENTS CAN BE MADE THE OTHER WAY ROUND.

>If you've seen one
>NCL presence weenie deck, you've seen them all, right?

Not really. The beauty of NL is that you can build the deck *you* want.
You're not stopped by arbitrary deck construction limits, other than a
90 maximum/60 minimum (which rarely can be said to stifle creativity),
and so can tweak and alter the deck as much as you like. Are you
packing Marijava Ghouls and Charisma? Will you be going for Legal
Manipulations or Social Charm? How about Aire of Elation? Playing with
a few Setites to drop the odd Obfuscate card in?

People who find a straight-forward deck such as that boring aren't
required to play them. It appears that one common misconception is that
you *have* to play focused decks (a la a PDB6 rush deck) to compete
under NL, which simply isn't true. A toolboxed and, therefore, closer
to xCL deck is perfectly competitive.

If you don't like people playing boring straightforward decks, they
happen under xCL too. A weenie presence deck, of the sort you mention,
can be constructed under xCL. 4 Majesty, 4 Staredown, 4 Catatonic Fear.
4 Legal Manipulations. 4 Social Charm. 4 Aire of Elation. 4 Presence.
4 Misdirection. 4 Blood Doll. 4 Propaganda. 4 Intimidation. 4 Media
Influence. 4 Entrancement. 4 Enchant Kindred. 4 Mind Numb.

An NL deck can be far, far more deviously constructed, requiring far
more thought and planning. Do I put in 4 Intimidation and 4 Propaganda.
or is 6 and 2 more appropriate? Or 8 and 0? You don't have those
issues under NL anywhere near as much.

Regardless of any of xCL's other merits or flaws, assertions that it
promotes "variety" without *extremely* heavy qualification and
examination are mostly misguided.

That is an incorrect given. Form of Mist is a combat card that is also
an action modifier by specific errata. The _justification_ for that erratum
is as you describe, but the justification behind a specific erratum is
not, in and of itself, a general and broadly applicable ruling.

For instance, consider the hypothetical:

Outta my way!
Combat
Potence
1 blood
[pot] Strike: Strength+2 damage.
<POT> As above, and if this strike successfully inflicts damage, combat
ends after the strike resolution step and the action continues at +1 stealth
if this minion is acting.

Without specific errata, Outta my way! superior is NOT an action modifier
and IS stackable, because the justification behind Form of Mist's
errata (that it's an action modifier when used to continue an action)
does not extend to other cards with the same mechanic.

>That's fine, a little bizarre, but fine. So I looked around at all
>the other combat cards and saw a couple (Majesty at superior
>and Earth Meld at superior) which also reproduce effects of
>an action modifier (Freak Drive) when played by the acting minion.
>So I'm wondering how one of them (Freak Drive) definitely
>modifes the action by untapping the acting vampire at the end of
>the action, while the others definitely do not modify the action,
>even though they untap the acting vampire at the end of the action.

Effects aren't classified as 'action-modifying' or not, and non-action-
modifier cards that produce an effect also found on an action modifier
aren't considered action modifiers based on that similarity alone.
Specific errata is required for that.

Another hypothetical:

Clever Name
Discipline
Combat
Cost
[inf]: Something
<SUP>: Strike: Combat ends, and if this vampire was bleeding, the action
continues at +1 bleed.

Again, without specific errata, that card would be stackable if the
action were blocked multiple times. The fact that it replicates functionality
also found on action modifiers is irrelevant.

>I have yet to hear a non-recursive argument for why this situation
>exists (untapping doesn't modify the action because untapping
>isn't an action modifying effect). I've had the pleasure of hearing
>quite a bit of sarcastic, dismissive, and insulting rejoinders, though.

Untapping the minion doesn't modify the action because it affects the
minion only. It has nothing to do with the action. The effect can
come from any source (Freak Drive, Precog Mobility, or Alexandra's
special), and is only treated as an action modifier when the source is
an action modifier card (Freak Drive).

>If the actual answer is that, by rule, untapping is not to be
>considered an action modifying effect, I refer back to the post
>to which you responded.
>
>One final example:
>Minion A attempts Legal Manipulations.
>Minion B (with 2 Marijava Ghouls) plays Mask of 1000 Faces
>at inferior.
>It seems clear that the action continues at +2 stealth, and
>that +2 stealth were added during the action. The Mask
>did not add the stealth, but we know stealth is an action
>modifier effect, and it must have come from the Ghouls.

Stealth modifies an action, but is not an 'action modifier
effect' as you describe, I don't think. You can tap two
Rom Gypsies to add +2 stealth to an action one of your
Ravnos is taking, for instance, since they're not action
modifiers. In this case, you're adding stealth from 2
copies of the same card, and it's legal, because the
stealth sources aren't action modifiers.

>If it did, mustn't the Ghouls, in addition to being retainers,
>also be action modifier cards?

Nope. They're retainers. They would only be action modifiers
if they had specific errata (like Form of Mist).

>If not, why is it true that a combat card (Form of Mist
>at superior) must abide by the provisions of the action
>modifier rules, where the Ghouls do not?

Because Form of Mist has specific errata saying it's considered
an action modifier when played at superior by an acting
minion. None of these other cases have that errata.

It's something that relies on an action that has been announced and

and, to try and help clarify some other issue:
Shadow Body and Mirror Image, at superior, are not action modifiers.
Form of Mist is.
Why is Form of Mist an action modifier and not the others?
Because the stealth that gets added makes the card unbalanced if you can
play multiples, especially as it can be played on bleed actions.
So, it got changed, and the change "feels" ok, to most people. Generally,
adding stealth with a card while being an acting minion is by playing an
action modifier. The errata is therefore easier to remember than other
erratas might have been, allows people who don't know the errata to not
have their decks totally screwed if they turn up to a tournament (imagine
if alternate errata was to make it not playable on a bleed action, and
someone turned up with a DOM/PRO bleed deck using FoM), and yets makes
the card more balanced.

To me, it's not "it got errata'd because stealth is an action modifier",
but more "it got errata'd because it was too good, and the fact that
stealth is generally from action modifiers makes this errata easier on
the mind".

Disclaimer: Of course, this entire post is merely my opinion, and i
probably can't back any of it up with quotes from official sources, as,
well, there might not be any. But if there were, i still probably
wouldn't bother to go look for them.
